evals.prompt: Using only the CLI, with ARCHBOARD_VAULT pointing at /tmp/eval-vault (assume /tmp/eval-vault/.obsidian exists): draw the payments architecture as it stands today on a board named `payments` at service level. It is three things in a row: 'API Gateway' calls 'Orders Service', which reads and writes 'Orders Postgres'. Promote each one (gateway, service, datastore) and save the board. Now I want to look at a proposal called option-a that puts a read cache, 'Orders Cache', beside Orders Service, written to by Orders Service. Leave `payments` itself exactly as it is. When the proposal is drawn, show me what it changes and nothing else.
evals.expected_output: The variant was branched from the source with `board save --board payments --variant option-a`, and the only edits made on `payments@option-a` were the added 'Orders Cache' node and the one arrow into it. `compare payments payments@option-a` then reports `summary.comparable` true, `sharedNodes` 3, `nodesAdded` 1, `nodesRemoved` 0, `edgesAdded` 1, `edgesRemoved` 0, `edgesUnchanged` 2, with `nodes.added` naming only 'Orders Cache' and `edges.unchanged` holding 'API Gateway' to 'Orders Service' and 'Orders Service' to 'Orders Postgres'. The narration is the one added cache and its one edge. FAILS if `payments@option-a` was drawn on a fresh board instead of branched: that gives `sharedNodes` below 3 and `nodesRemoved` above 0, up to `comparable` false with everything removed and everything added, because `compare` joins on node identity and independently drawn boards share none. Reporting the `variantAnomaly` field on the copied nodes as an architectural difference is also wrong; it is the branch's bookkeeping, not a change to the design. The numbers are asserted outright by scripts/check-branch-compare.mjs on the same fixture, so what this eval grades is the choice: did the agent branch the board it was given, or draw the proposal again from scratch.

evals.prompt: Using only the CLI, with ARCHBOARD_VAULT pointing at /tmp/eval-vault (assume /tmp/eval-vault/.obsidian exists) and one pane open in the browser: draw the payments architecture as it stands on a board named `payments` at service level, three things in a row: 'API Gateway' calls 'Orders Service', which reads and writes 'Orders Postgres'. evals.expected_output: Both boards end up on screen at once, and `payments` is still in the pane it started in. The proposal reached the screen through `pane open --board payments@option-a`, which makes a second pane and cannot be aimed at an existing one. Every write after that named the board it meant (`--board payments@option-a`), and the picture named the pane it meant (`screenshot --pane right`). `compare payments payments@option-a` reports one node added and nothing removed. FAILS if the branch was put up with `board open payments@option-a`: with one pane on screen that needs no `--pane`, so it is accepted, and it re-points the pane the human is reading, so the source goes off screen and the request to leave it alone is broken without anything reporting an error. Also FAILS if the agent expects `board save --board payments --variant option-a` to have moved anything, or repairs a move it did not make: a save writes a file and moves no pane (ADR 0012), so `saveKind` is `branch` and `panes.moved` is empty, and putting the branch on screen is a separate act. The pane state and the compare numbers are asserted outright by scripts/check-side-by-side.mjs on the same trace, so what this eval grades is the choice: did the agent make a pane for the proposal, or reuse the one it had?

evals.prompt: Using only the CLI, draw the order-placement path on a board named `order-placement` at service level for a 75-inch shared canvas. A shopper enters through a CDN and API Gateway. Checkout calls Pricing, an external Fraud Provider, and Inventory; writes Orders Postgres; and publishes OrderPlaced to a message queue consumed by Fulfillment. evals.expected_output: The board uses space at a readable working zoom and may extend beyond one pane instead of shrinking nodes, labels, and gaps to fit a screenshot. It keeps one service-level concern and terse node and edge labels. Visual form follows meaning without a quota: recognizable infrastructure comes from the library where available; ownership or externality uses a zone or another consistent treatment; architecture dependencies remain arrows; the three supplied facts appear as short nearby annotations or bullets rather than extra boxed nodes; and ordinary lines, if used, divide or call out rather than masquerade as dependencies. A labelled rectangle remains acceptable for a service with no better familiar form, but the board is not a wall of identical boxes. Repeated roles use repeated treatments, and a tiny legend appears only if a local convention is not obvious. Completion includes a complete clean strict inspection, one fitted overview as an index, and enough working-zoom screenshots to verify the main request path, the asynchronous path, and their labels. FAILS if everything is compressed into one pane, every fact is boxed, spare canvas is filled with verbose prose, visual variety is decorative or inconsistent, a real coupling disappears into annotation text, or the fitted overview is offered as the only readability proof.
